item.title: ORACLE: Binding Query Parameters with ODPNET by Name
item.description: ORACLE: Binding Query Parameters with ODPNET by Name In this post, we will discuss the issue of binding query parameters by name with Oracle’s ODP.NET provider. Many developers prefer to use the Microsoft ADO.NET provider for Oracle because it binds parameters by name instead of by position. Although, the Microsoft provider is soon to be deprecated, and developers should switch to Oracle’s ODP.NET provider. The problem with ODP.NET is that it defaults to binding parameters by position, which can lead to bugs and make it harder to write parameterized queries.

item.title: How to Prevent SQL Injection in Oracle's Order By Clause
item.description: Preventing SQL Injection in Oracle “ORDER BY” Query with NamedParameterJdbcTemplate When creating an SQL query with a sorting “ORDER BY” part, it’s crucial to prevent SQL Injection attacks. This is done by using parameter maps to prevent injection in the “where” part of the query. One approach is to use MANUAL escaping, but this could be challenging for more complex parameters.

item.title: Maximizing Efficiency with Oracle Identity Columns and Insert Into Select
item.description: Maximizing Efficiency with Oracle Identity Columns and Insert Into Select Oracle Identity Column: Insert Into Select In Oracle 12, a new feature of Identity Columns was introduced, which allows automatic generation of primary key values. item.description: ORACLE: Get N Rows from Dual with SQL Query How to generate N rows from dual using SQL query? If you want to write a SQL query that accepts a bind variable and its output consists of one column and N number of rows, each row having its row number, you can use the below query: SELECT level AS val FROM dual CONNECT BY LEVEL <= :NUM; Here, the :NUM is a bind variable that you can pass the value of N, and the CONNECT BY LEVEL is used to generate N rows from the dual table.

item.title: Oracle's Guide to DDL and Transaction Rollback
item.description: Oracle’s Guide to DDL and Transaction Rollback Is DDL transactional in Oracle? DDL (Data Definition Language) statements in Oracle, such as Create or Alter, are not transactional. According to Oracle’s official documentation, the database implicitly commits the current transaction before and after every DDL statement. Essentially, DDL statements act as separate transactions to any data modifications that the statement may make. While other transactions may make modifications involving the object being modified in a DDL statement, all these operations will still run in the transaction that includes the DDL statement.
